summary: Route Flap Damping was proposed to reduce BGP churn, but it was found to penalize well-connected sites, and many operators turned it off. Based on measurement, this document recommends new parameters that make damping usable.

eli5.summary: A rule meant to calm a noisy path was punishing good places. This suggests gentler settings so people can use it again.

questions: what suppress threshold should i use for bgp damping
why did operators turn off route flap damping
what is the bgp maximum penalty
subtitle: Gentler Route Flap Damping settings that quiet the worst BGP flappers without punishing well-behaved prefixes.

tldr.problem: Route Flap Damping was meant to reduce BGP churn, but it severely penalized well-connected sites, and many operators turned it off.
tldr.mechanism: Based on measurements, the RFC recommends raising the router's maximum penalty to at least 50,000 and setting the suppress threshold to no less than 6,000 (or 12,000 for conservative operators).
tldr.outcome: Only the most frequently flapping prefixes are damped, so some long-term churn is cut without disturbing normal convergence. The RFC calls this minimal change, not a panacea.

today: RFC 7196 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It recommends parameter values rather than a new protocol.

sections.title: Why Damping Fell Out of Favor
sections.content:
Route Flap Damping (RFD) was proposed and implemented to reduce BGP churn in routers. Unfortunately it was found to severely penalize sites for being well connected, because topological richness amplifies the number of update messages exchanged. Many operators turned RFD off.

Measurements cited by the RFC showed that very few prefixes cause a large share of BGP messages: in one week-long experiment at a router with feeds from a Tier-1 provider and an Internet Exchange Point, only 3% of the prefixes produced 36% of the BGP messages. Only these very frequent flappers should be damped.

The goal is stated modestly: with absolutely minimal change, reduce the danger of current RFD implementations and use. It is not a panacea, nor a deep approach to flap reduction. Readers are assumed to know BGP (RFC 4271) and Route Flap Damping (RFC 2439).
sections.eli5: A safety rule made to calm noisy network paths ended up punishing paths that were just busy. People switched it off, and this RFC tries to make it safe to switch back on.

sections.title: The RFD Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC lists the parameters common to all implementations. Some can be tuned by the operator and some cannot. It notes there is currently no consensus on a single set of default values, and shows the defaults of two vendors.

The penalty constants for a withdrawal, a re-advertisement and an attribute change are not tunable. The suppress threshold, half-life, reuse threshold and maximum suppress time are tunable. Values without units are dimensionless constants.
sections.eli5: Every time a route misbehaves it gets points. Some point amounts are fixed and some knobs, like how many points trigger a time-out, can be turned by the operator.

sections.title: Suppress Threshold versus Churn
sections.content:
The RFC reports measurements from a week between September 29, 2010 and October 6, 2010. With a suppress threshold of 6,000, the BGP update rate was estimated to drop by 19% compared with no RFD, and 90% fewer prefixes were damped than with the 2,000 threshold. Far fewer well-behaved prefixes are damped.

At 12,000, only 0.22% of the prefixes were damped, which still gave an average hourly update reduction of 11% compared with no RFD. The table in the RFC notes that the current default suppress threshold of 2,000 is overly aggressive.
sections.eli5: If you give a time-out after only a few mistakes, lots of kids get one. If you wait for many mistakes, only the real troublemakers do, and things are still quieter.

sections.title: The Maximum Penalty
sections.content:
The parameters in the first table and the implementation's sampling rate impose an upper bound on the penalty value, which the RFC calls the computed maximum penalty. In addition, BGP implementations have an internal constant, the maximum penalty, which the current computed penalty may not exceed.

This matters because a high suppress threshold is useless if the penalty can never climb that high. That is why the recommendations raise the internal constant.
sections.eli5: If the scoreboard stops at 2,000 points, you can never reach a time-out line set at 6,000. The scoreboard has to be able to count higher.

sections.title: The Recommendations
sections.content:
Section 6 recommends the following values.

  • Router maximum penalty: the internal constant MUST be raised to at least 50,000.
  • Defaults: existing implementations SHOULD NOT change their default values, so as not to break existing operational configurations.
  • Minimum suppress threshold: operators wanting damping that is much less destructive than today's, but still somewhat aggressive, SHOULD set it to no less than 6,000.
  • Conservative suppress threshold: conservative operators SHOULD set it to no less than 12,000.
  • Calculate but do not damp: implementations MAY offer a test mode that shows the results of a configuration without damping any prefixes, so parameters can be tuned without losing reachability.
sections.eli5: Make the scoreboard count much higher, leave the factory settings alone, and tell operators to pick a much higher time-out line. A practice mode lets them try it safely.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: An attacker can generate false flapping to cause a victim's prefixes to be damped. Because the recommendations only move parameters to more conservative values, the RFC expects no increase in risk, and says the change should slightly mitigate the false-flap attack.
sections.eli5: A bully could fake misbehavior to get someone a time-out. A higher bar makes that trick a bit harder.
